To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the biotechnology faculty in agricultural colleges are relatively new to their discipline, have more industrial funding and involvement than their non‐agricultural counterparts, and are more optimistic about the possible positive benefits of that involvement.

the land-grant agricultural colleges are becoming more involved with industrial funding of biotechnology research, that this funding is associated with lower university productivity and less university funding, and that this industrial funding has not had the negative effects on faculty attitudes toward industrial funding that have been observed in the non-land-grant university biotechnology community.

the land-grant agricultural colleges of biotechnology faculty are younger, more involved in industry, and more positive about industry's involvement in university research than their counterparts in nonagriculturally oriented research universities.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the impact of industrial involvement in university research.
the changing nature of the university and with the changing role of the land-grant agricultural college in the new bioscieties.
the effects of biotechnology on the traditional missions and activities of the agricultural colleges and the effects of industrial involvement on university research.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the land-grant college of agriculture biotechnology faculty have a higher level of industrial involvement than the nonagricultural faculty and that industrial funding has a negative impact on university productivity.
the land-grant biotechnologists are more involved with industry and are more positive toward industrial funding than the nonagricultural biotechnologists.

the land-grant agricultural colleges are more active than nonagricultural universities in biotechnology research, but the differences are small and may reflect differences in the way that biotechnology research is funded and supported in the agricultural colleges.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the land‐grant colleges of agriculture have been able to adapt more readily to the new biotechnology and to the new industrial involvement in biotechnology research than have nonagricultural universities.
land‐grant agricultural colleges are more likely to be affected by industrial involvement in the biotechnology research of their faculty than nonagricultural universities.
industrial funding has had a significant positive impact on the biotechnology research of land-grant colleges, but the effect has not been without cost.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the agricultural college biotechnologists appear to have more recently received the highest degrees and are more involved in industrial activities than nonagricultural biotechnologists.
the agricultural colleges are not as well positioned to compete with nonagricultural universities in the biotechnology field as they were in the agricultural field.
industrial funding is a significant factor in the activities of agricultural biotechnology faculty.
